docs.title: nolainocr
docs.text:
nolainocr turns a stack of similar documents — invoices, receipts, purchase orders, bank statements, forms — into a table you can export. You upload a PDF or images at nolainocr.com, wait while each page is read, and download Excel, CSV, JSON, or Google Sheets.

The unusual constraint is layout. Pages in one run should share a template. The service learns the fields from the first page and applies that shape to the rest, so “Invoice No.”, “Ref.”, and “Bill Number” land in one column instead of three.

This documentation is for people who want to use, evaluate, or understand nolainocr. It does not describe how to run the service from source. Choose the route that matches your goal; each route starts with the least context it requires.

docs.title: Use nolainocr
docs.text:
1. Follow Extract your first documents to create an account at nolainocr.com and finish one extraction.
  2. Continue with Common workflows for batches, template groups, and export.
  3. Check Plans and page limits before estimating a month of work. Current prices are on the pricing section.
  4. The troubleshooting guide covers common user-facing failures.

If you only have twenty minutes, read this page, Extract your first documents, and the opening of How nolainocr is built.

docs.title: Understand nolainocr
docs.text:
Start with How nolainocr is built for the four layers and the decisions that steer cost, quality, and trust. Then read The parts of the system for component responsibilities and A job from start to finish for one representative end-to-end flow.

After that foundation, use Accounts and access, Billing and pages, and Design choices to examine three deeper mechanisms. Data and privacy states what the product promises about documents and payments.

docs.title: Browse the documentation
docs.text: The chapters move from first use to the conceptual model, then to policy.

docs.title: 1. Getting started
docs.text:
• Extract your first documents — account, first upload, first table
  • Common workflows — batches, pages-per-document, export
  • Plans and page limits — what you pay for, and how far a month of pages goes
  • Troubleshooting — user-facing diagnosis and recovery
  • Free tools — browser utilities that do not require an account

docs.title: 2. Policies
docs.text: • Data and privacy — session files, payment handling, and the public privacy policy

docs.title: 3. How it works
docs.text:
• How nolainocr is built — the product bet, the four layers, and the invariants
  • The parts of the system — the website, the extraction engine, identity, and settlement
  • A job from start to finish — one batch, walked through every turn
  • Accounts and access — sign-in, email verification, and session cleanup
  • Billing and pages — monthly quota, top-ups, and when a page is counted
  • Design choices — why the product looks this way

docs.title: A few words you will meet again
docs.text:
Here is some glossary you will find useful to browse through the documentation.

Word Meaning in this book Page One image the extractor reads. A five-page PDF is five pages. Session The working set of uploads and results while you are signed in. Files are removed when you log out. Template group How many consecutive pages make one document (1–4) when a PDF mixes several receipts or invoices. Schema The field names learned from the first page and applied to the rest of the batch. Page quota The monthly allowance on your plan, consumed before any purchased top-up pages.

docs.title: Free tools
docs.text: nolainocr.com/tools is a set of browser utilities that run on your device. They do not require an account and they do not send files through the extraction service. Use them to reshape a PDF or image before you upload a batch, or for small tasks that never need OCR.

docs.title: When to use them
docs.text:
If a vendor PDF mixes layouts, split it. If you have many one-page invoices as separate files, merge them. If a scan is rotated or in the wrong image format, fix it here, then continue on the dashboard.

None of these tools consume page quota.

docs.title: What is on the tools page
docs.text:
Group Tools PDF Merge, split, PDF to images and back, delete pages Image Resize and crop, rotate, convert format Data JSON formatter, CSV to Markdown, text diff, text stats Utility QR code, currency converter, world time

The live list is always the tools index.

docs.title: Related tasks
docs.text:
• After the file is the right shape, follow Common workflows.
  • These utilities are also listed for crawlers in the site’s llms.txt.

docs.title: Plans and page limits
docs.text: nolainocr sells pages, not files. A page is one image the extractor reads. This page explains what that unit means for a month of work. Current prices and numeric allowances are published on nolainocr.com; treat that section as the live catalog.

docs.title: What you pay for
docs.text:
Three kinds of capacity exist:

Kind What it is Free plan A small monthly allowance so you can try the product without a card. Paid monthly plans Higher pages per document and per calendar period (Pro and Pro Plus). Top-up packs Extra pages you buy once. They are used after the monthly allowance is exhausted.

A run can be refused for either of two independent caps:

  • Pages per document — how large one file (or one logical document) may be.
  • Pages per month — how many pages the plan still has in the current period.

Both are visible on your account after sign-in.

docs.title: How a page is counted
docs.text:
Pages are billed when extraction finishes, not when you upload. A file you preview and discard does not consume the monthly allowance. A successful extraction of a ten-page PDF consumes ten pages.

Monthly quota is consumed first. Top-up pages are consumed only after that quota is empty. If both are empty, the dashboard asks you to upgrade or buy a pack instead of starting the job.

Period renewal resets the monthly counter. Unused top-up pages remain as overflow; they are not the same bucket as the plan allowance. The precise settlement rules are in Billing and pages.

docs.title: Choosing a plan
docs.text:
If you process a handful of documents to evaluate quality, stay on Free until you hit a cap. If a typical vendor PDF is longer than the free per-document limit, you need a paid plan even for a single file.

For a repeating monthly load — invoices, receipts, statements — compare your expected page count with the allowances on the pricing section. Top-up packs cover a spike without changing plan. For a workflow the self-serve product does not cover, contact describes custom extraction work.

docs.title: Manage billing in the product
docs.text:
1. Open nolainocr.com/account.
  2. Review current plan, usage, and top-up balance.
  3. Upgrade, change plan, open the Stripe customer portal, or cancel at period end.

Payment card data never enters nolainocr servers; Stripe collects it. See Data and privacy.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
• If a limit blocked a run, recover in Troubleshooting.
  • If you are planning architecture rather than a purchase, continue with How nolainocr is built.

docs.title: Troubleshoot the dashboard workflow
docs.text: Use the message visible on nolainocr.com to choose a recovery path. These steps stay on the user side: they restore a normal workflow without exposing service credentials or operator procedures.

docs.title: You cannot open the dashboard
docs.text:
Visible symptom: sign-in succeeds but the dashboard sends you back to verify email, or login is rejected.

  1. If you registered with email, open the verification message and follow the link, then sign in at nolainocr.com/login.
  2. If the message never arrived, wait a few minutes, check spam, and retry from the verification screen.
  3. Use Forgot password when the password is the problem. Reset links expire; request a new one if the form rejects the token.

Google sign-in goes through Google’s consent screen and returns to nolainocr. If that loop fails, try email sign-in or contact with the approximate time — not your password.

docs.title: Upload is refused
docs.text:
Visible symptom: the dashboard rejects the file, or extraction never starts.

  • Use PDF, JPEG, or PNG.
  • Confirm the file is under the size the upload control accepts. Very large scans may need to be split with the free PDF tools first.
  • Confirm the page count is within your plan’s per-document cap. The account page shows the current limit.

docs.title: Extraction stops on a plan limit
docs.text:
Visible symptom: the product says you are out of pages, or asks you to upgrade.

Monthly quota is used before top-up pages. If both are empty, open Account, upgrade or buy a pack, then retry. A preview of pages does not itself consume allowance; a finished extraction does. See Plans and page limits.

docs.title: The table looks wrong
docs.text:
Visible symptom: columns duplicate, names are noisy, or two document types are mixed in one sheet.

The batch must share a layout. Split unrelated templates into separate runs. If one PDF interleaves two-page documents, set pages per document to match the repeating unit (1–4) and extract again. Reset the dashboard between unlike batches so the previous schema does not linger in the session.

docs.title: Progress sits still on a large job
docs.text:
Visible symptom: a multi-page run shows a progress indicator for a long time, then completes or fails.

Large stacks are processed in the background so the browser is not left waiting on a single request. Stay on the dashboard until the results panel fills. If the job fails, retry once. If it fails again, contact with the approximate time and the visible error text. Do not include document contents.

docs.title: Export is empty or Google Sheets does not open
docs.text:
Visible symptom: download produces no useful file, or the Google Sheets path asks for permission and stops.

Extract successfully before export. Excel and CSV come from the current results table. Google Sheets needs a Google account permission in the browser; deny or block that prompt and the send will not finish. Retry after granting access, or download Excel instead.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
• Re-run a clean batch with Common workflows.
  • Read A job from start to finish if you want to know which stage failed conceptually.

docs.title: Extract your first documents
docs.text: nolainocr is a hosted service. This guide takes you from a browser to a downloadable table using nolainocr.com. You do not need this repository.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • a browser
  • an email address, or a Google account
  • one PDF or image whose pages share a layout — a short stack of invoices or receipts is enough

Supported uploads are PDF, JPEG, and PNG. Pages in the same run should look like the same form. If you have two layouts, split them into two files and run each separately; see Common workflows.

docs.title: Create an account
docs.text:
1. Open nolainocr.com/register.
  2. Register with email and password, or choose Google.
  3. If you registered with email, open the verification message and follow the link before you try the dashboard.

Sign-in afterwards is at nolainocr.com/login. The free plan does not require a card. Current paid plans and page allowances are on the pricing section.

docs.title: Upload and extract
docs.text:
1. Open nolainocr.com/dashboard. A short tutorial highlights the three panels: upload, configuration, results.
  2. Drop a PDF or images onto the upload area. The dashboard shows page previews when the file has more than one page.
  3. If each invoice or receipt is a single page, leave pages per document at 1. If one document spans two pages, set that number to 2 (up to 4).
  4. Choose Extract Data.

A single page returns a table on the same screen. A multi-page job shows progress while pages are read, then fills the results panel. A successful run ends with columns you can scan, copy, or download.

The first page teaches the field names. Later pages are aligned to that shape, including labels that mean the same thing in different words.

docs.title: Export the table
docs.text: From the results panel, download Excel or CSV, copy JSON, or send the table to Google Sheets. That file is yours; the uploaded pages are not a permanent archive. They belong to the session and are deleted when you log out. See Data and privacy.

docs.title: Know the current boundary
docs.text:
nolainocr extracts structured fields from documents that repeat a layout. It does not classify mixed piles, join unrelated templates in one run, or keep a long-lived document warehouse after logout.

If extraction refuses the file, hits a plan limit, or the table looks wrong, use the matching steps in Troubleshooting before trying a larger batch.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
• Repeat the flow with a realistic stack in Common workflows.
  • Check Plans and page limits before a full month of invoices.
  • Read How nolainocr is built if you want the layers behind this screen.

docs.title: Common workflows
docs.text: Once an account can complete one extraction, the dashboard covers a small set of repeated jobs. This page is the task list; the first-run path is Extract your first documents.

docs.title: Extract a stack of the same layout
docs.text:
Use this when every page is the same kind of document — fifty supplier invoices, a folder of receipts, a multi-page bank statement.

  1. Sign in at nolainocr.com/dashboard.
  2. Upload one PDF that contains all the pages, or several images.
  3. Keep pages per document at 1 unless each logical document spans more than one page.
  4. Choose Extract Data and wait for the table.
  5. Export Excel, CSV, JSON, or Google Sheets.

Expected result: one row (or one row-group) per document, with shared column names. If two vendors use unrelated templates, split the file and run twice; mixed layouts in one batch produce messy columns.

Industry-specific examples live on the solutions pages: invoices, receipts, purchase orders, bank statements, accounting, logistics, and insurance.

docs.title: Group pages that belong to one document
docs.text:
Some PDFs interleave two-page invoices or a cover sheet plus a detail page. The dashboard calls this a template group: how many consecutive pages make one document.

  1. Upload the PDF.
  2. Set pages per document to 2, 3, or 4 to match the repeating unit.
  3. Extract.

Expected result: each group is treated as one document, not as unrelated singletons. The limit is four pages per document. Larger multi-page packets need to be split first, or run as page-by-page extraction if each page is itself a complete record.

docs.title: Export and start over
docs.text:
The results panel is the working table for this session.

  • Excel / CSV — download a spreadsheet.
  • JSON — copy structured data.
  • Google Sheets — send the table to a sheet you authorize in the browser.
  • Reset — clear the dashboard and upload the next batch without logging out.

Logging out is different from reset: logout deletes the uploaded files from the service. If you still need the originals, keep them on your computer; nolainocr is not a document store. Details are in Data and privacy.

docs.title: Change plan or buy extra pages
docs.text:
When a run is blocked because the monthly allowance or the per-document page cap is exhausted:

  1. Open nolainocr.com/account.
  2. Upgrade or change plan, or purchase a top-up pack of extra pages.
  3. Return to the dashboard and retry.

Card details are collected by Stripe, not by the dashboard. How quota and top-ups combine is in Plans and page limits and Billing and pages.

docs.title: Related tasks
docs.text:
• Recover from a failed run in Troubleshooting.
  • Merge or split PDFs first with the free tools if the file is the wrong shape for one batch.

docs.title: Data and privacy
docs.text: nolainocr is built so that using the product does not require leaving a permanent copy of your documents on the service. This page states that policy in product language. The legal text is the privacy policy.

docs.title: Documents live in a session
docs.text:
When you upload a PDF or images, the service keeps those files only long enough to extract and to show previews. That working set is the session. Logging out deletes the uploads. Extracted tables that you export are files on your computer or Google account; they are not kept as a document archive after logout.

Do not treat the dashboard as storage. If you need the originals tomorrow, keep them locally.

docs.title: What else is collected
docs.text:
The privacy policy lists the categories. In short:

Category Why it exists Account information Email, and Google profile fields if you sign in with Google Uploaded documents Temporary input for extraction Extracted data Shown in the session so you can export it Billing status Plan, usage, and whether a subscription is active — not card numbers Usage and technical data Page counts for limits; ordinary server logs

Payment card details are collected by Stripe and never stored by nolainocr. Transport uses TLS.

docs.title: What we do not do with documents
docs.text:
The privacy policy states that documents and extracted data are not sold and are not used for advertising. Extraction is performed to return a table to you. Identity and billing records exist to run the account.

For rights, retention, and contact, use the privacy policy and contact.

docs.title: Where this sits in the architecture
docs.text: Session-scoped files are an invariant of How nolainocr is built, not an afterthought in operations. The next chapter names the parts that enforce it.

docs.title: Accounts and access
docs.text:
Settlement starts with who is calling. This chapter explains sign-in, verification, and what logout does to the session. It does not explain how operators wire an identity vendor; that stays in the private book.

If you have not read The parts of the system, start there.

docs.title: Ways to sign in
docs.text:
nolainocr offers email and password, and Google. Both end in the same place: a verified account that can open the dashboard and account screens.

Email registration creates the login, sends a verification message, and attaches a free plan so the first extraction has a quota to spend. Until the email is verified, those screens redirect you to finish verification.

Google uses Google’s consent screen and returns to nolainocr with a session. The account still receives a plan record; there is no second product for OAuth users.

Password reset is a mail loop: request from Forgot password, open the link, choose a new password, sign in again. Links expire; request another if the form rejects the token.

docs.title: What the session is for
docs.text:
After sign-in, the website keeps you authenticated so uploads and extractions are attributed to your plan. The document session is separate in kind: it is the files sitting on the service so the dashboard can preview and extract. Logout ends both. Uploaded pages are deleted; you return to the public site.

Resetting the dashboard between batches clears the working table without signing you out. That is the right control when you have a second layout to process in the same sitting.

docs.title: What this is not
docs.text:
There is no public integration API in this documentation, and no user-issued API keys to paste into other software. Access is the website session. Maintainers who change authentication internals use the private book in this repository (docs-private/).

Protected product behavior — verified email, session-scoped files, plan gating — is part of the identity of How nolainocr is built. Changing those rules is a product change, not a silent implementation tweak.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Billing and pages is the other half of settlement: quota, top-ups, and Stripe. Data and privacy restates what logout promises.

docs.title: Billing and pages
docs.text:
Settlement’s other half is what a page costs you. This chapter is the policy model: monthly quota, top-ups, and when a page is counted. Numeric prices live on the pricing section. How to click through checkout is in Plans and page limits.

If you have not read The parts of the system, start there.

docs.title: Two pools, one priority
docs.text:
Every account has a monthly page quota from its plan (free or paid). It may also hold top-up pages bought as one-time packs.

When extraction completes, pages are subtracted from the monthly quota first. Only when that quota is empty do top-up pages move. If both are empty, the next job is refused rather than run.

This priority is an invariant: top-ups are overflow, not a way to skip the plan. Period renewal resets the monthly counter; leftover top-up pages remain until they are used.

docs.title: When a page is counted
docs.text:
A page is work the extraction layer finished. Upload and preview do not settle. A failed job should not be assumed to consume pages; check Account if you need the authoritative usage number.

Per-document caps are a separate gate. A file that is legal on Pro can be illegal on Free even when monthly quota remains, because one PDF is too long for that plan.

docs.title: How money enters the picture
docs.text:
Paid plans and top-up packs are purchased through Stripe Checkout. After payment, Stripe tells nolainocr to activate the plan or add overflow pages. The account screen can also open the Stripe customer portal for invoices, cards, plan changes, and cancellation at period end.

nolainocr stores that you are on a plan and how many pages you have used. It does not store card numbers. That split is the same trust boundary as in Data and privacy.

docs.title: What you see versus what operators see
docs.text: Users see prices, remaining pages, and Stripe-hosted checkout. How payments are confirmed internally belongs in the private book (docs-private/). If a public sentence needs a secret name or a database field to be useful, it is in the wrong book.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Design choices explains why pages (not files or seats) are the product unit. Troubleshooting covers a run blocked by empty pools.

docs.title: Design choices
docs.text:
Earlier chapters stated how the system behaves. This chapter names the bets that make that behavior look inevitable — and where those bets stop applying. It is not a catalog of libraries.

If you want the layer map first, start with How nolainocr is built.

docs.title: Same layout, not mixed piles
docs.text:
The product assumes a batch is one template. That yields aligned columns and an honest failure mode: split the folder. A classifier that sorts mixed documents in one upload would be a different product, with different errors and a different price.

Consequence: users are asked to prepare the stack (including the free tools when a PDF is the wrong shape). The engine is not asked to be a mailroom.

docs.title: Session files, not a document CMS
docs.text:
Keeping uploads only for the session reduces retention and disk. It also means nolainocr is a processor, not a filing cabinet. Logout is a delete. If you need history, you export.

A saved-project library existed in earlier thinking and is not the current dashboard. Do not expect named archives to reappear without a product change.

docs.title: Hosted vision, not classical OCR alone
docs.text: Field extraction is done with a hosted vision model that returns structured data, not with a local character engine that only dumps text. The gain is semantics and tables; the cost is vendor dependence and per-page spend. Settlement charges pages because that is the unit the model (and the user) actually consume.

docs.title: Semantic columns, not exact labels
docs.text: Once the schema exists, later pages are allowed to use different words for the same box. The table stays usable in Excel. The failure mode is occasional over-merge. Exact string matching would produce cleaner uniqueness and worse spreadsheets.

docs.title: Background jobs for stacks, immediate return for one page
docs.text: A single image can finish while you wait. A stack cannot rely on one browser request. Progress on the dashboard is therefore part of the architecture, not decoration. Closing the tab early can mean you miss the result even if the job still finishes on the server — stay until the grid fills, then export.

docs.title: Pages and plans, not seats
docs.text:
Pricing is built around pages per document and pages per month, plus optional overflow packs. That matches invoice-heavy months better than per-seat SaaS. It also makes the free tier a real trial: a short PDF fits; a two-hundred-page statement does not.

Live numbers stay on nolainocr.com so this book does not drift from the catalog.

docs.title: Browser tools stay local
docs.text: Merge, split, and image utilities run in the browser so they can be free, logged-out, and off the extraction bill. They are adjacent product, not a back door into orchestration.

docs.title: Where this model stops
docs.text:
• Unstructured essays, photos with no form, and mixed mail need a different pipeline.
  • Organizations that must keep a server-side archive need a different retention policy than logout-deletes-files.
  • Teams that need an API rather than a dashboard are outside this public book; contact is the path for custom work.

Maintainer alternatives (other queues, databases, or OCR vendors) live in the private book (docs-private/) because they name implementations.

docs.title: A job from start to finish
docs.text:
The previous chapter named the parts. This chapter follows one realistic batch through them: a twelve-page PDF of same-layout invoices, two pages each, exported to Excel.

If you have not read The parts of the system, start there. This is not a click-by-click tutorial; that is Extract your first documents.

docs.title: The scene
docs.text: You are signed in, email verified, on a plan that allows a twelve-page file. The PDF contains six invoices, two pages each, all from the same template. You want one spreadsheet.

docs.title: 1. Upload
docs.text:
The dashboard sends the PDF to orchestration. Orchestration checks file type and page count against the plan, converts each PDF page into an image the extractor can read, and stores those images in the session. The website shows previews.

Nothing has been billed yet. You could log out and the files would be deleted.

docs.title: 2. Configure the repeating unit
docs.text:
You set pages per document to 2. That template group tells extraction to treat pages 1–2 as invoice A, 3–4 as invoice B, and so on. Leaving the control at 1 would have produced twelve thin records instead of six documents.

This is still orchestration: it is a parameter on the job, not a new product.

docs.title: 3. Start the job
docs.text:
Choosing Extract Data admits the work. For more than one image the engine runs in the background. The website opens a progress channel and draws a bar. You keep the dashboard available so results can arrive.

Settlement is consulted here only as a gate: if quota and top-ups are already empty, the job is refused before pixels reach the vision model.

docs.title: 4. Schema from the first document
docs.text:
The extraction layer reads the first group (pages 1–2) and proposes field names — invoice number, date, vendor, lines, totals. That list is the schema for the rest of the PDF.

If the first document is a cover sheet with a different layout from the invoices, the schema will be wrong for the stack. That is a preparation mistake, not a hidden setting: put a representative page first, or split the file.

docs.title: 5. Remaining pages
docs.text:
Later groups are read into the same columns. Nested objects become flat names (vendor + name → a vendor-name column). Labels that mean the same thing are aligned so the sixth invoice does not create a private extra column for “Inv. #”.

Large stacks may spend longer in this stage; progress ticks as groups complete.

docs.title: 6. Settle pages
docs.text:
When the table is ready, settlement counts the pages that were processed and subtracts them from monthly quota, then from top-up pages if needed. The account screen’s usage number moves.

If the job fails before completion, treat the usage figure on Account as the source of truth for whether pages were charged. The product intends to bill completed extraction.

docs.title: 7. See and export
docs.text: The results grid fills. You download Excel. That file is now on your computer. Logging out deletes the session images; it does not retract the spreadsheet.

docs.title: Other journeys, same skeleton
docs.text:
Journey What changes What does not Single image No background job; the table returns on the same request Schema, session, page billing Many one-page receipts Template group stays 1 Same-layout rule Sign-up then first extract Identity and a free plan record are created first Extraction still session-scoped Hit a limit Orchestration refuses at the gate You change plan or top up, then retry Logout Session files go away Plan and usage remain

Password reset, Google sign-in, and Stripe checkout are settlement side-quests. They are specified in Accounts and access and Billing and pages, not in this pipeline.

docs.title: Where a job can stop
docs.text:
• Before upload: wrong file type, too many pages for the plan.
  • Before extraction: no remaining pages.
  • During extraction: provider or job-queue failure; retry, then contact support with the time and the on-screen error.
  • After extraction: export is a client action; an empty grid means the job did not actually complete.

User-facing recovery is in Troubleshooting.

docs.title: The parts of the system
docs.text:
The previous chapter explained why nolainocr is split the way it is. This chapter is a map of what sits on each side of that split: the website, the extraction engine, identity, and settlement.

If you have not read How nolainocr is built, start there. The words page, session, schema, template group, and page quota are used here with the meanings that chapter introduced.

This chapter defines the running components and their boundaries. The next chapter owns the job-by-job walkthrough.

docs.title: One browser, one service
docs.text:
When you extract a stack of invoices, your browser talks to a hosted service. Nothing in this public book is a local engine you install. The product is the website and the work it starts on your behalf.

The website is what you see: landing and solutions pages, sign-in, dashboard, account, blog, and free tools. It does not perform OCR in the browser for the paid extraction path. It uploads pages, shows previews and progress, and renders the table.

The extraction engine is the hosted worker that reads pages. It is the only part that sends document pixels to a vision model, aligns columns, and returns structured rows. Multi-page jobs run in the background so a long stack does not depend on a single request staying open.

Around that engine sit four supporting roles:

  • A job queue — holds work and progress so the website can show a bar instead of spinning on one HTTP call.
  • Identity — who you are, whether email is verified, whether the session is valid.
  • Account records — plan, usage, top-up balance.
  • A payment provider (Stripe) — checkout, customer portal, and subscription events. Card data stays there.

A health check exists for operators. Users see success as a filled results table, not as an infrastructure dashboard.

docs.title: Layers and components
docs.text:
Browser
  → website (experience)
      → orchestration (upload, limits, job, progress)
          → extraction engine (schema, pages, table)
      → settlement (identity, plan, Stripe)
Part Layer Owns Does not own Marketing, blog, solutions, tools Experience Explaining the product; browser-only utilities Extraction quality; billing Dashboard Experience Upload, configuration, results, export Model calls; card collection Account screens Experience Showing plan and starting checkout Webhook bookkeeping Orchestrator Orchestration File acceptance, page caps, job lifecycle Schema invention Extraction engine Extraction Vision read, flatten, align columns Who pays Identity provider Settlement Sign-up, login, password reset, Google Document pixels Plan ledger Settlement Quota, top-ups, period OCR accuracy Stripe Settlement Cards, invoices, portal Document storage

The free tools at nolainocr.com/tools stay on the experience layer and never enter orchestration. That is why they do not consume pages.

docs.title: What the extraction engine produces
docs.text:
The primary result is always a table: named columns and values ready for Excel, CSV, JSON, or Google Sheets. Everything else is supporting machinery.

Stage Consumes Produces User-visible? Accept file PDF or images Session pages and previews Upload panel Learn schema First page Field names for the batch Implicit in column headers Read remaining pages Later pages + schema Per-page records Progress on large jobs Align and flatten Nested or variant labels Rectangular columns The results grid Settle pages Completed page count Updated quota Account usage

Optional artifacts such as a saved “project library” are not part of the current product. The dashboard works on the session in front of you; export is how results leave.

docs.title: Trust and failure boundaries
docs.text:
• Transport. The site is served over HTTPS in production.
  • Documents. Visible to the extraction engine for the session; deleted on logout.
  • Accounts. Email/password or Google. Protected screens require a verified email.
  • Payments. Stripe checkout and portal; nolainocr records plan state, not PAN/CVC.
  • Capacity. If monthly quota and top-ups are empty, orchestration refuses the job rather than running extraction for free.
  • Layout. Mixed templates fail as poor tables, not as a silent rewrite into a different product.

When the vision provider or the job queue is unavailable, large extractions fail in the dashboard. Retry once, then contact with the time and the visible error. Internal recovery is a maintainer concern.

docs.text: A job from start to finish walks one batch through these parts. Accounts and access and Billing and pages zoom in on settlement. Maintainers with repository access continue in the private book (docs-private/ in this repository), which is not published with this chapter.

docs.title: How nolainocr is built
docs.text:
This chapter explains the product bet, why responsibilities are split across four layers, and which invariants and trade-offs follow. The next chapter names the components; the workflow chapter owns the page-by-page journey.

You do not need to know the codebase. By the end you will have a small vocabulary — page, session, schema, template group, page quota — and a picture of four layers that everything else hangs on.

docs.title: The core bet
docs.text:
Imagine a folder of supplier invoices. You want a spreadsheet of invoice numbers, dates, totals, and line items. You do not want to type them. You also do not want a tool that only works if every vendor used the same PDF generator.

nolainocr’s bet is: same layout, structured extraction.

You upload pages that share a template. The service reads the first page well enough to name the fields — that list of names is the schema — then reads the rest of the batch into those columns. Labels that mean the same thing in different words are merged so the table stays rectangular enough to export.

The analogy is a clerk and a stack of identical forms. You do not hire someone to invent a new filing system per sheet. You show one filled example; the clerk copies the boxes onto every following page. Mixed forms in one stack defeat the clerk. Two stacks, two runs, two clean tables.

That constraint is the product. Everything below is how the constraint is kept reliable, cheap enough, and hard to misuse.

docs.title: Four layers
docs.text:
Think of four floors, from closest to you to farthest from the document pixels.

Experience layer      the website: landing, dashboard, account, tools, export
Orchestration layer   accepts uploads, enforces limits, runs jobs, reports progress
Extraction layer      turns pages into structured records and aligns columns
Settlement layer      who you are, which plan you are on, what the pages cost

The document plane is experience + orchestration + extraction: take pages, return a table. The control plane is settlement: identity, quota, payment. Uploaded files never become a long-lived warehouse; they belong to a session and leave when you log out.

docs.title: Experience layer
docs.text:
The experience layer is nolainocr.com: marketing and solutions pages, sign-in, the dashboard, account and billing screens, the blog, and the free browser tools.

It does not read document pixels, charge pages, or decide schema. This keeps the browser a client of the service, while accepting that a multi-page job cannot finish inside one short HTTP request — progress has to come back to the screen.

docs.title: Orchestration layer
docs.text:
The orchestration layer treats an upload as a job, not as an unbounded chat. It checks that the file type and page count are allowed, stores pages for the session, starts extraction, and streams progress until a table is ready.

It does not invent field names or talk to the card network. The gate saves wasted model calls when a plan is exhausted, but it means a preview is not yet a billable page — only a finished extraction is.

docs.title: Extraction layer
docs.text:
Once a job is admitted, the extraction layer turns each page into structured data. The first page proposes the schema. Later pages are read into that shape. Nested values are flattened into spreadsheet columns. Names that are close in meaning are unified so “Ref.” and “Invoice No.” do not become two sparse columns.

It does not own identity or prices. Quality depends on scan quality and on the same-layout rule; a mixed stack is out of scope, not a prompt to be clever.

docs.title: Settlement layer
docs.text:
The settlement layer identifies the caller, exposes plan limits, and charges pages when extraction completes. Monthly quota is consumed before top-up pages. Card data is collected by the payment provider, not by this layer’s document path.

Charging by completed page follows useful work, so an abandoned upload does not spend the month. Two similar-looking PDFs can still differ in page count, and therefore in cost.

docs.title: Durable invariants
docs.text: The implementation can evolve without changing the product’s identity only while these boundaries remain true.

docs.title: Documents are session-scoped
docs.text:
• Uploads exist to be extracted, not to be archived.
  • Logout deletes the working files.
  • Exports you download are yours; they are not a second copy the service keeps as a library.

Because extraction must read pixels, documents do leave your laptop for the duration of the session. That is data minimization in time, not a claim that pages never transit the service. The legal detail is Data and privacy.

docs.title: Layout is a batch contract
docs.text:
• One run assumes one template.
  • A template group (1–4 consecutive pages) is how a repeating multi-page document is described, not a way to mix unrelated forms.
  • The schema is learned from the start of the batch and applied forward.

If a change requires the extractor to classify an arbitrary mixed pile in one click, it is fighting this design.

docs.title: Pages are the unit of settlement
docs.text:
• Limits are pages per document and pages per month.
  • A page is counted when extraction finishes.
  • Quota before top-up; refusal when both are empty.

docs.title: Payments stay at the payment provider
docs.text:
• Plan and usage records live with the account.
  • Card numbers do not.

docs.title: Trade-offs that follow
docs.text:
Same-layout batches over mixed-document intelligence. The table is cleaner, and the product is honest about when to split a folder.

Session files over a document CMS. Disk and retention stay small; users must keep originals themselves.

Async jobs over one blocking request. Large stacks can finish without the browser timing out; the dashboard must stay open enough to receive progress.

Semantic column alignment over exact string matching. “Total” and “Amount due” can merge; occasional over-merging is the cost.

Hosted vision over local classical OCR. Structured JSON and language coverage come with vendor cost and rate limits. The design choices chapter names that bet without turning it into a vendor scorecard.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: The parts of the system places website, engine, identity, and settlement on this four-layer map. A job from start to finish walks one batch across the boundaries.
